dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Hello, what would you like to drink?

dialogue.speaker: Zainab
dialogue.english: Hi, do you have coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، شلون تحبها، وسط لو سادة؟
dialogue.transliteration: akeed, shlon ti7ibha, wasat lo saada?
dialogue.english: Sure, how do you like it, medium or plain?

dialogue.speaker: Zainab
dialogue.english: Medium, please.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Okay, I'll get it ready now.

dialogue.speaker: Zainab
dialogue.english: Is there sugar on the table?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: No, I'll bring it to you now.

dialogue.speaker: Zainab
dialogue.english: Thank you, may God give you health.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Here you go, your coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Zainab
dialogue.english: Bless you, it's really nice.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Enjoy (lit. with wellness).

pair.english: What would you like to drink?

response.english: Mint tea, if there is any.

pair.english: Do you like it sweet or plain?

lessons.culture: Offering tea to a guest is the first move of Iraqi hospitality, and chaay (strong, sweet, in a small waisted glass called an istikaan) is far more common than coffee in most homes and cafes. Iraqi coffee, gahwa, is the small bitter cup served at gatherings and after meals.

exercises.prompt: شتريد تشرب؟ (shtreed tishrab?)

too_formal.item: أرغب في فنجان من القهوة من فضلك
too_formal.feedback: That is Modern Standard Arabic; nobody says it that way at a cafe table.

exercises.tip: law sama7t is the everyday word for please.

exercises.prompt: أكو سكر؟ (aku sukkar?)

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but too stiff for a quick answer across a cafe table.

exercises.tip: hassa means right now.

exercises.prompt: أريد چاي ___ (areed chaay ___ na3na3), with mint

too_formal.feedback: ma3a is the MSA word for with; Iraqi fuses bi + al into one word.

exercises.tip: bi- is glued to the noun, there is no separate word for with.

exercises.prompt: گهوة ___ (gahwa ___), meaning plain, no sugar

too_formal.feedback: Bookish description; saada is the one word everyone uses.

exercises.tip: saada is used for coffee and tea alike.

exercises.prompt: Coffee with no sugar at all.

too_formal.item: قهوة من غير أي سكر على الإطلاق
too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine MSA, but nobody strings it together this formally in speech.

exercises.tip: abad at the end means at all, it strengthens the no.

exercises.prompt: I want mint tea.

too_formal.feedback: arghab is textbook Arabic; Iraqis say areed for I want, and mean it politely.

exercises.tip: areed is the everyday I want in Iraqi, not rude.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'bitter coffee'?

too_formal.feedback: Overexplained; murra alone does the job in speech.

exercises.tip: murra also means bitter for any taste.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask 'what would you like to drink?' to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA question, too formal for a waiter chatting with a customer.

exercises.tip: The -een ending marks that you are speaking to a woman.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I like my coffee bitter.

too_formal.feedback: MSA phrasing; the dialect says I like the coffee bitter directly.

exercises.tip: murra comes last, describing how you like it.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: A big cup of coffee.

too_formal.feedback: Fine MSA order but not how it is said casually.

exercises.tip: kbeer (big) comes after the whole phrase finjaan gahwa.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you, where is the menu?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: And upon you peace, here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.transliteration: il yoom 3idna simach masgoof w kabaab
dialogue.english: Today we have masgouf fish and kebab.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.arabic: إي، أكو دولمة وشوربة عدس وفتوش
dialogue.transliteration: ee, aku dolma w shorbat 3adas w fattoosh
dialogue.english: Yes, there is dolma, lentil soup and fattoush.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: The masgouf is really good with us.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.arabic: مو حار، بس أكو شطة على الجنب
dialogue.transliteration: mu 7aar, bass aku sha66a 3ala l janib
dialogue.english: Not spicy, but there is chili on the side.

pair.english: Do you have an English menu?

response.english: We have masgouf fish and kebab.

pair.english: Is it spicy or not spicy?

lessons.culture: Masgouf, river fish split open and grilled beside an open fire, is Baghdad's signature restaurant meal, and it is usually ordered by weight. Prices are quoted in dinars, and people often say only the thousands, so five means five thousand.

exercises.prompt: أكو منيو بالانگليزي؟ (aku menu bil ingleezi?)

too_formal.feedback: MSA and stiff; a waiter just says aku, hassa.

exercises.tip: aku means there is; maaku means there isn't.

exercises.prompt: حار لو مو حار؟ (7aar lo mu 7aar?)

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but Iraqis say mu for not, not laysa.

exercises.tip: mu (not) goes right before the word it negates.

exercises.prompt: ___ عدكم اليوم؟ (___ 3idkum il yoom?), what

too_formal.feedback: maadha is MSA; Iraqis say shinu for what.

exercises.tip: shinu is what in Iraqi; it opens most questions.

exercises.prompt: ___ منيو بالانگليزي؟ (___ menu bil ingleezi?), is there

too_formal.feedback: hal yujad is MSA; aku is the Iraqi there-is.

exercises.tip: aku is the most Iraqi word there is; it works for anything you are looking for.

exercises.prompt: Is there vegetarian food?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but it sounds like a written notice.

exercises.tip: akil means food; it also covers a dish.

exercises.prompt: I want something light.

too_formal.feedback: Right in MSA; the dialect says shee, not shay'an.

exercises.tip: shee is the short everyday word for thing.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks 'How much is this?'

too_formal.feedback: kam si3r hadha is MSA; Iraqis just say beesh.

exercises.tip: beesh is the market word for how much.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks 'What's in this dish?'

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but stiff for a quick question to a waiter.

exercises.tip: haay is this for a feminine noun such as akla.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Is there a dish of the day?

too_formal.feedback: Textbook style; the dialect keeps it to four words.

exercises.tip: aku always leads the question.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: What do you recommend I get?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA; the dialect drops the that-clause and joins the words.

exercises.tip: sh- plus tinsa7ni is what-you-advise-me, one breath.

phrases.transliteration: haadha l 6abaq ili w haadha ilha

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Are you ready to order?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Yes, I want a plate of hummus and fattoush.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: And for the main course?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.transliteration: areed haadha, w marti treed haadha
dialogue.english: I want this one, and my wife wants this one.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Okay, anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.arabic: خبز زايد، وأگدر آخذ كلاص ماي؟
dialogue.transliteration: khubz zaayid, w agdar aakhuz glaas maay?
dialogue.english: Extra bread, and can I have a glass of water?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sure, I'll bring it now.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.arabic: بعد شوية: طلبنا ما وصل لهسه
dialogue.english: A bit later: our order hasn't arrived yet.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Sorry, it's coming now, two minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Can you repeat the order so we're sure?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.arabic: حمص وفتوش، ومشاوي مرتين بدون بصل
dialogue.transliteration: 7ummus w fattoosh, w mashaawi marratayn bidoon basal
dialogue.english: Hummus and fattoush, and grilled meat twice without onion.

response.english: Yes, I want kebab and salad.

lessons.culture: Iraqi tables fill up with shared plates and stacks of samoon or khubz, so asking for zaayid (extra) bread is normal and never rude. Water is called maay, and a polite no-more is tislam, yikfi (thank you, that's enough).

exercises.prompt: جاهز تطلب؟ (jaahiz ti6lub?)

too_formal.item: نعم، أرغب في طبق من الكباب
too_formal.feedback: MSA; at a table people say ee and areed.

exercises.tip: ee is the Iraqi yes, the same as na3am but softer.

exercises.prompt: شي ثاني؟ (shee thaani?)

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but flat and formal at a meal.

exercises.tip: tislam (may you be safe) is a warm thank you.

exercises.prompt: بدون ___ (bidoon ___), without onion

too_formal.feedback: duuna is MSA; bidoon is what is said.

exercises.tip: bidoon goes straight before the noun.

exercises.prompt: أگدر آخذ ___ ماي؟ (agdar aakhuz ___ maay?), a glass of water

too_formal.feedback: ka's is MSA; Iraqis borrow English and say glaas.

exercises.tip: maay is Iraqi for water; glaas maay is a glass of water.

exercises.prompt: Extra bread, please.

too_formal.item: من فضلك أضف المزيد من الخبز
too_formal.feedback: Too wordy; Iraqis just name the thing and add zaayid.

exercises.tip: zaayid means extra, more than usual.

exercises.prompt: My order hasn't arrived yet.

too_formal.feedback: lam yasil is MSA; the dialect uses ma plus the past verb.

exercises.tip: lihassa means until now, so not yet.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'Without onion, please'?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but bidoon plus law sama7t is what is said.

exercises.tip: basal is onion; bidoon is without.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks 'Can you repeat the order?'

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA; tigdar is the natural can you.

exercises.tip: gaf becomes g in Iraqi: tigdar, not taqdir.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: We want the same order.

too_formal.feedback: Formal phrasing; nafs before the noun is the everyday order.

exercises.tip: nafs (same) goes before the noun.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: I'll have a plate of hummus and fattoush.

too_formal.item: أود تناول طبق من الحمص والفتوش
too_formal.feedback: Too literary; areed plus the plate is all you need.

exercises.tip: The plate word comes first, then the two dishes joined by w.

phrases.transliteration: y3a6eek il 3aafya, il akil chaan lazeez

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Right away, I'll bring it now.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Twenty-five thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.english: No, I'm paying today.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.arabic: لا والله، آني أدفع، إنت دفعت المرة اللي فاتت
dialogue.transliteration: la wallah, aani adfa3, inta dafa3it il marra illi faatat
dialogue.english: No, I swear, I'm paying, you paid last time.

dialogue.speaker: Ali
dialogue.english: Okay, shall we split the bill?

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.english: Fine, do you take cash or card?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.arabic: كاش لو كارت، مثل ما تريدون
dialogue.transliteration: kaash lo kaart, mithil ma treedoon
dialogue.english: Cash or card, as you like.

dialogue.speaker: Saad
dialogue.transliteration: agdar aakhuz il wasil? w khalli l baagi
dialogue.english: Can I have the receipt? And keep the change.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Thank you, God keep you.

response.english: Right away, I'll bring it now.

pair.english: Bless your hands, the food was delicious.

response.english: God keep you safe, enjoy it.

lessons.culture: Arguing warmly over who pays is a normal Iraqi ritual, and insisting aani adfa3 (I'm paying) is a sign of generosity, so expect the other person to protest too. Tislam eedak (bless your hands) is the compliment to whoever cooked, and the answer is bil 3aafya or alla ysallmak.

exercises.prompt: شكد الحساب؟ (shgad il 7isaab?)

too_formal.feedback: Full MSA form; a waiter says just the number.

exercises.tip: 3ishreen (twenty) is the Iraqi form, not 3ishroon.

exercises.prompt: تسلم إيدك، الأكل لذيذ (tislam eedak, il akil lazeez)

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; bil 3aafya is the warm everyday reply.

exercises.tip: bil 3aafya means with wellness, said to someone eating.

exercises.prompt: ___ لو سمحت (___ law sama7t), the bill

too_formal.feedback: faatoora is understood, but 7isaab is what Iraqis ask for.

exercises.tip: 7isaab literally means account or reckoning.

exercises.prompt: اليوم آني ___ (il yoom aani ___), I'm paying

too_formal.feedback: sa-adfa3u ana is MSA; the plain present adfa3 already means I'm paying.

exercises.tip: aani is the Iraqi I; adding it stresses that it is you.

exercises.prompt: Keep the change.

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA; khalli is what is said when leaving change.

exercises.tip: baagi means the rest, also used for the change from a note.

exercises.prompt: Can I have the receipt?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but far too stiff for a cafe.

exercises.tip: wasil is the Iraqi receipt; agdar aakhuz is can I take.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'Shall we split the bill?'

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA; the dialect says nigsim with a g sound.

exercises.tip: nigsim starts with n-, the we form.

exercises.prompt: Which one asks 'Is there a discount today?'

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA, but aku is what is actually said.

exercises.tip: takhfeed and khasim both mean discount.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: No, I'm paying.

too_formal.feedback: kalla and sa-adfa3 are MSA; la, aani adfa3 is spoken.

exercises.tip: la comes first, then aani, then the verb.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: Is there a tip included in the bill?

too_formal.feedback: Correct MSA; bakhsheesh is the everyday word for a tip.

exercises.tip: bil (in the) is glued to 7isaab.

challenge.title: At the Restaurant
challenge.instructions: Have a full conversation ordering a drink and a meal at an Iraqi restaurant, then ask for and settle the bill.
required_elements: Ask what's on the menu or what's recommended
Order at least one drink and one dish, including one preference (e.g. no onion, extra bread, sweet or plain)
Ask for the bill and how much it costs
Say something to close the meal, like a compliment to the food or a thank you

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.english: What do you recommend I get?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: The masgouf is really good with us.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.transliteration: tamaam, areed masgoof w chaay wasat
dialogue.english: Okay, I'll have masgouf and a medium-sweet tea.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: With onion or without?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.english: Without onion, please.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: Okay, coming right up.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.english: The bill, please.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.english: How much is the bill? Twenty thousand.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.arabic: تسلم إيدك، الأكل چان لذيذ هواية
dialogue.transliteration: tislam eedak, il akil chaan lazeez hawaaya
dialogue.english: Bless your hands, the food was really delicious.
